title: For heaven's sake (Avot 2:12)
hook: let your friend's property be as dear as your own, and do everything for heaven's sake

segments.voice: Yesterday, ayin tovah: Rabbi Joshua warned against the begrudging eye. Your line was glad when others do well.

Oh, for heaven's sake. It comes out when the printer jams, when the dog gets into the trash, when someone takes the last parking spot. It's what people say when they're fed up. Hebrew has a phrase with almost the same words. Leshem shamayim, for the sake of heaven, isn't a sigh of frustration at all. It's a way of living. And it comes from Rabbi Yose, the student his teacher called the pious one.
screen: `OH, FOR HEAVEN'S SAKE.` → `A SIGH, OR A WAY OF LIVING?` → `RABBI YOSE, THE PIOUS ONE.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Yose says three things. First: let your friend's property be as dear to you as your own. Treat the borrowed ladder like it's yours. Better, actually, because it isn't. Return it on time, clean, working. Second: prepare yourself to learn Torah, because it isn't an inheritance. You can inherit a house from your parents, but not their learning. Even the child of the greatest scholar starts from the first page and does the work himself. Third: let all your deeds be for the sake of heaven. Heaven, here, is a respectful way of saying God. Whatever you do, let it point toward something higher than yourself. Not only praying and studying. Everything. Later Jewish teachers took this very far. Maimonides wrote that even eating and sleeping can be for the sake of heaven, if you do them to keep your body healthy so you can do good. The meal is still a meal. The nap is still a nap. What changes is the reason. Put the three together. Other people's things matter as much as yours. What's worth having has to be earned, not handed down. And ordinary life can be aimed at something holy, printer jams and parking lots included. Even the moment you want to say oh, for heaven's sake can remind you what the Hebrew phrase means.
screen: `YOUR FRIEND'S THINGS AS YOUR OWN.` · `LEARNING ISN'T AN INHERITANCE.` · `ALL YOUR DEEDS FOR HEAVEN.` · `EVEN EATING AND SLEEPING.` · then, large: `FOR HEAVEN'S SAKE.`

segments.voice: Think of something completely ordinary you'll do today: making lunch, commuting, answering email, returning something you borrowed. Ask what higher purpose it could serve: feeding someone well, getting somewhere to help, keeping a promise. You don't have to change the act; just let the reason point a little higher.
Leshem shamayim. For the sake of heaven: Rabbi Yose's teaching that all your deeds, even the ordinary ones, can be done for the sake of heaven.
Your line: return it in good shape. A borrowed ladder can point toward heaven too. Day two hundred sixty, done.

howItsDone: The phrase leshem shamayim is used for acts done with a higher purpose, and some Jews say a short declaration of intention before performing a commandment.

chat.meaning: Rabbi Yose said let all your deeds be for the sake of heaven. Even a meal or a nap can aim higher; what changes is the reason.

leshem shamayim.meaning: for the sake of heaven, meaning for God's sake

Rabbi Yose.meaning: the student his teacher called the pious one

Maimonides.meaning: a great medieval Jewish philosopher and legal scholar

Torah.meaning: teaching: the Five Books, and Jewish learning as a whole

notes: Avot is paraphrased (outline follows Taylor 1897). Numbering: 2:12 common, 2:17 in some editions.
Maimonides on eating and sleeping for the sake of heaven: Hilkhot De'ot 3:2–3; also Shulchan Aruch Orach Chayim 231; confirm.
Rabbi Yose called 'pious' (chasid) by Yochanan ben Zakkai in Avot 2:8.
The claim that the English exclamation 'for heaven's sake' derives from the Hebrew is NOT made; the script only contrasts the two. Keep it that way.
howItsDone mentions declarations of intention (leshem yichud) said by some before mitzvot; confirm phrasing.
